tourTitle: Baroque Bratislava: Palaces, Cloisters and Quiet Lanes

stops.title: Michael's Gate and Michalská Street
stops.why: Gather under the last surviving city gate, whose Gothic tower was given its bulbous Baroque onion cap in the 1750s. From here Michalská runs south lined with noble town palaces, including the Palace of the Hungarian Royal Chamber where the Diet met, the Segner house and the tiny walled-in St Catherine's Chapel; the narrow Baštová lane beside the ramparts is the quietest corner in the old town.

stops.title: Great Evangelical Church, Panenská
stops.why: A short climb outside the walls to a hushed Lutheran quarter. The Great Evangelical Church (1774-76) is austere late Baroque, built under Josephine rules that forbade towers and street doors - a fine lesson in how faith shaped facades. The neighbouring Lyceum courtyard is usually empty.

stops.title: Župné námestie and the Capuchin Church
stops.why: The plain Baroque Capuchin church of St Stephen with its Marian plague column in front - votive Baroque at its most modest. The square sits just off the traffic, and Kapucínska and Klariská lead away into the stillest streets of the historic core.

stops.title: Kapitulská and the Clarissine Convent
stops.why: The canons' street: almost car-free, walled gardens, the Renaissance Emericanum college and the Provost's Palace with its St Elizabeth group carved on the spot. Beside it the Clarissine church, whose Gothic shell hides the Baroque and Rococo refitting of the convent - the quietest stretch of the walk.

stops.title: St Nicholas Church on the Castle Road
stops.why: A tiny whitewashed church on the old road up the hill, standing above the vanished Jewish quarter. We keep to the terrace here rather than climbing to the castle, and look out over rooftops with almost nobody around.

stops.title: St Martin's Cathedral and the House of the Good Shepherd
stops.why: The coronation church of Hungarian kings, with its Baroque St Martin equestrian group by Georg Raphael Donner inside. Across Rudnayovo square stands the House of the Good Shepherd, the narrowest and most delicate Rococo house in the city, plus the Csáky Palace and the old Salvator pharmacy.

stops.title: Ventúrska Street: the palace row
stops.why: One paved lane, four aristocratic palaces: Pálffy, Zichy, the de Pauli Palace with its garden pavilion where the child Liszt performed, and the late-Baroque Erdődy Palace at the corner. The medieval Universitas Istropolitana courtyard is a step away and rarely busy.

stops.title: Hlavné námestie at the Roland Fountain
stops.why: The main square, best read from the fountain: the Old Town Hall tower, the Jesuit church with its Marian column, the Rococo Kutscherfeld Palace (smallest in the city), Jesenák and Palugyay houses, and the Vice-Governor's Palace. A single sweep of Baroque and Rococo facades around one open space.

stops.title: Panská Street and Hviezdoslav Square
stops.why: Panská, the old 'Lords' Street', keeps the Balassa Palace and the pocket-sized Baroque Corpus Christi chapel wedged between houses; the Pálffy Palace stands at the corner. We finish the leg under the plane trees of Hviezdoslav Square by the Ganymede fountain and the old theatre - shady and calm at the edges.

stops.title: Franciscan and Primate's Squares
stops.why: The finale for a Baroque eye: Mirbach Palace, the city's finest Baroque-Rococo house with its original panelled rooms, the oldest church in town beside it, the Ursuline Loreto church, and the pink Primate's Palace whose enclosed courtyard with the St George fountain is the calmest place to end.
